senses: Touchy, aggressive or confrontational, usually while drunk.
ety: Variation of leery, originally Cockney slang.
examples: There's always been a weird duality at the heart of New Order: the fact that three druggy, lairy Mancs and the drummer's girlfriend can craft music of such awesome emotive power as to make grown neds weep.
Unskinny was a self-published riot of large lasses getting lairy in northern towns, and did a reasonable trade via friends and comic shops.
The show is lairy, loud and laddish; it does exactly what it says on the tin.

senses: Renewal, revival.
ety: From renascent + -ence.
examples: Ignored by her own time, Dickinson was sentimentalized in her renascence.

senses: Having many spines.
Spine-like; spiny.
ety: From spine + -ous, or borrowed from Latin spinōsus.
examples: The organs are simple and spinous, the spines small distally on the organ, larger proximally.

senses: A litter of piglets.
ety: From Middle English *farow, *fargh (found only in the plural faren), from Old English fearh (“piglet”), from Proto-West Germanic *farh, from Proto-Germanic *farhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos, from *perḱ- (“to dig”). See also Old High German farah, Middle Irish orc (“piglet”), Latin porcus, Proto-Slavic *porsę (“pig, piglet”), Lithuanian par̃šas, Avestan: 𐬞𐬆𐬭𐬆𐬯𐬀 (pər^əsa). Doublet of pork.
examples: Aha! I know you, gammer! Hamlet, revenge! The old sow that eats her farrow!
At full speed he ran into a pigsty, where a sow was lying on her side with a farrow of eleven tugging at her.
She is the womb and the tomb: the sow that eats her farrow.

senses: The state of being an athlete, or of taking part in athletic events.
A show of athletic prowess.
ety: From athletic + -ism.
examples: It catches an American athleticism and energetic team spirit that still seem to smash European notions of ballet classicism, as does its dancers’ selfless manner and their practicelike costumes.
Both Alcaraz and Sinner pushed themselves - and each other - to the limit in a classic contest that showcased all of their shot-making, athleticism and resilience.

senses: Having, or being full of, holes.
ety: From Middle English holy, holi, holly, holli (“holey, spongy, hollow”); equivalent to hole + -y. The e was inserted in Modern English to distinguish the word from holy (“hallowed, sacred”).
examples: Fred loved holey Dutch cheese.
Steven also acknowledged that his presentation of self—wild locs, nerd glasses, and holey hipster jeans for our first interview—encourages whites to speak to him.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of junk; cheap, worthless, or of low quality.
Full of junk.
ety: From junk + -y (adjectival suffix).
examples: I took my jewelry box & made a bracelet for Jim from an old broken necklace & the clasp from a junky charm bracelet.
We really need to clear out the junky basement.

senses: A person who seethes.
ety: From seethe + -er.
examples: The following strategies can help a seether gain control of angry feelings.
Oh, she is not born like other girls / But I know how to conceive her / Oh, she may not look like other girls / But she's a snarl-toothed seether, seether!

senses: A place where people or things stay temporarily.
An enclosed or fortified prehistoric site, especially a European Iron Age hill-fort.
A meeting (especially an annual meeting or important conference) of an outdoorsy group of people, such as military veterans or scouts of the scouting movement.
The act of encamping or setting up a camp; also, the state of being encamped or in a camp.
ety: From encamp (“to establish a camp or temporary shelter”) + -ment (suffix forming nouns denoting actions or their results).
examples: As Carriere, the Canadian straggler did not make his appearance for two days after the encampment in the valley, two men were sent on horseback in search of him. They returned, however, without success.

senses: A craftsman who lays, or repairs roofs.
A daredevil who performs stunts on tops of skyscrapers.
ety: From roof + -er.
examples: Ivan, Kirill and Vasilisa are “roofers,” a loose-knit group of insanely non-acrophobic daredevils who scam and sneak their way to the tops of Russia’s highest buildings.
Many people say that I don’t look like roofer, which is really good when I try to get into a building which is really good secured. I started roofing two years ago with some friends.

senses: A piece of hard candy on a stick; a lollipop.
An ice lolly; a popsicle.
Any confection made from sugar, or high in sugar content; a sweet, a piece of candy.
ety: A clipping of lollypop.
examples: Leaving the Domain, I walked back to the hotel, noticing the queer signs by the way. One was “Lollies for Sale.” It was over the door of a confectioner′s store where all sorts of candies were displayed.

senses: Of or resembling a shrub.
Planted or covered with shrubs.
ety: From shrub + -y.
examples: A shrubby species suitable for beefarming, as it flowers profusely from November-January, and yields both pollen and nectar.

senses: A cool room in a domestic house where food is stored.
A food supply.
ety: Inherited from Middle English larder, from Anglo-Norman larder and Old French lardier, from Latin lardārium. By surface analysis, lard + -er.
examples: Many of these cones had opened, and nuthatches visited the tree frequently to take seeds from the squirrel's larder.

senses: The distinctive pattern of hairline cracks in the surface of an old painting.
ety: Borrowed from French craquelure.
examples: Alan squinted. It was the robot, the one he’d given her, the pretty thing with the Dutch Master craquelure up its tuna-can skirts.

senses: An obelisk or upright stone pillar, usually as a primitive commemoration or gravestone.
ety: From Latin stēla, from Ancient Greek στήλη (stḗlē). Doublet of stele.
examples: In the courts of the houses lie many round stelæ, or pillars, once placed on the graves of the Athenians.
He erected a stela, with an inscription in the sacred character, to commemorate his successes.
The upright blocks or stelas are among the most curious parts of the present ruin.

senses: A Mexican dish made by filling a tortilla with cheese and sometimes other ingredients and then cooking it until the cheese is melted.
A Salvadoran pan dulce made with rice flour and queso duro blanco and topped with sesame seeds.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish quesadilla. [Alt: Slices of a quesadilla piled on top of one another]
examples: In the Salvadoran bakery, the quesadilla is king, whether cut into squares from a cake tray or baked into discus-sized round coffee cakes.

senses: To become visible again by turning off a cloaking device.
ety: From de- + cloak.
examples: Romulan warbird decloaking alongside the Vulcan ships.

senses: A sexual encounter during lunch hour, especially one which is illicit.
ety: From noon + -er.
examples: A simple recess for lunch can turn into a nooner—a midday sexual encounter.
If you're going to knock off a nooner with a co-worker at a bad motel you have to scrawl your worn Hancock on the desk blotter.

senses: A road or track not following a main route; a secondary or minor road or path.
A road that is not frequently travelled.
a little-known or arcane field of study or detail.
ety: From Middle English bywey, equivalent to by- + way.
examples: Although some of its individuality has been lost, this railway byway in North Essex still retains its charm, and is well worthy of exploration by railway enthusiasts.
Though his account of written communication over the past 5,000 years necessarily has a powerful forward momentum, his diversions down the fascinating byways of the subject are irresistible ...

senses: To make something rational or more rational.
To justify a discreditable act, or irrational behaviour.
To structure something along modern, efficient and systematic lines, or according to scientific principles. This often includes eliminating duplication and grouping like or similar items.
ety: From French rationaliser. By surface analysis, rational + -ize.
examples: Vested interest, united ties, / landed gentry, rationalize. / Look who bought the myth. / By jingo, buy America.

senses: The liveliest part of something.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀορτή (aortḗ, “the arteries springing from the heart”), from ἀορτέω (aortéō), lengthened form of ἀείρω (aeírō, “to lift, raise”).
examples: Tracing their battles, I had many occasions to walk along Second Avenue, the aorta of the Lower East Side, exploring places that were once as vibrant and tumultuous as Midtown Manhattan.

senses: One of a race of people living in the extreme north, beyond the north wind.
ety: From Late Latin hyperboreanus, cognate with Classical Latin hyperboreus, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβόρεος (huperbóreos), composed of ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + βόρειος (bóreios, “northern”). By surface analysis, nearly hyper- + boreal. See also Ὑπερβόρεοι (Huperbóreoi).
examples: The Hyperboreans venerated Apollo over the other gods.

senses: To surgically remove a part of the body, especially a limb.
ety: From Latin amputō (“prune, cut away”). The original sense of pruning (a tree, etc.) became obsolete. The OED considers uses related to anything other than an animal limb to be figurative uses of the modern sense.
examples: The surgeon had to amputate the patient’s leg to save his life.
Several soldiers had limbs amputated after the battle.

senses: Pasta in the shape of short spirals.
ety: From Italian fusilli, plural of fusillo, diminutive of fuso (“spindle”).
examples: Fusilli is very good served with classic tomato sauces.

senses: To be quiet; to keep quiet.
To ask someone to be quiet, especially by saying shh.
ety: Imitative. Compare shh and hush.
examples: He wouldn't shush so I kicked him.
The boy in front of us was making too much noise, so we shushed him.

To this day, many in the spelling world rebuff supernatural claims: On the podcast, parents say that they’ve been “shushed” in online forums, or “shut down” from sharing their experiences at conferences.

senses: An executioner responsible for hanging criminals.
Someone responsible for hanging pictures and other artworks in a gallery, museum etc.
A guessing game where one has to guess the word an opponent is thinking of by guessing one letter at a time, and involving the gradual drawing of a stick figure hanging from the gallows.
ety: Inherited from Middle English hangman, hongman, hangeman, equivalent to hang + -man.
examples: One cried, "God bless us!" and "Amen" the other, As they had seen me with these hangman's hands.

senses: A proclamation, announcement or preaching.
An assertion or affirmation.
ety: From Middle English predicacion, from Anglo-Norman predicaciun, from Latin praedicātiō, from praedicō.
examples: It can be immediately observed from these sentences that the English subject of a predication is translated in Japanese with a wa-phrase, while the subject of a nonpredicational description appears as a ga-phrase.

senses: Having a full, voluptuous figure, especially possessing large breasts.
Full of health, vigour, and good temper.
ety: From Middle English buxom, also ibucsum, ibuhsum (“bendsome, flexible, pliant, obedient”), from Old English bōcsum, *būhsum, *ġebūhsum (“bendsome, pliant, obedient”), from Proto-West Germanic *beuhsam, *beugsam, equivalent to bow (“to bend, bow at the waist”) + -some or buck (“to bend, buckle, kick”) + -some. Cognate with Scots bowsome (“compliant”), West Frisian bûgsum (“flexible, bendy”), Dutch buigzaam (“flexible, pliant”), German biegsam (“flexible, pliant”).
examples: Aarfy's buxom trollop had vanished with her smutty cameo ring, and Nurse Duckett was ashamed of him because he had refused to fly more combat missions and would cause a scandal.
DIED. Robert Brooks, 69, canny businessman who, as chairman of Hooters, turned the bar-restaurant chain, famed for buxom waitresses in orange hot pants, into an international success.
He had not seen Zilla since Paul had shot her, and he still pictured her as buxom, high-colored, lively, and a little blowsy.

senses: To transform (or cause to transform) from a softer animal substance into bone; particularly the processes of growth in humans and animals.
To become (or cause to become) inflexible and rigid in habits or opinions.
To grow (or cause to grow) formulaic and permanent.
ety: Back-formation from ossification, or modeled on French ossifier and formed from Latin os, ossis (“bone”) + -ify.
examples: Before long, the entire organization ossifies.
Possession of absolute knowledge would ossify the human spirit, quenching human creativity;
This accidental repartition gets repeated, develops advantages of its own, and gradually ossifies into a systematic division of labour.

senses: A type of incense obtained from the Boswellia thurifera tree.
ety: From Old French franc encens (“noble incense”).
examples: Frankincense, Frankenstein, Francophile, Philistine / Frankly, we are killing time

senses: A mathematician who specializes in geometry.
ety: From Middle English gemeter, geometer, ultimately from Late Latin geōmetrēs, from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + μετρέω (metréō, “to measure”).
examples: But this idea, which is a general postulate in all demonstrations, has been taken for granted by every algebrician and geometer.

senses: Excellent, impressive.
Big, strong, durable, reliable, trustworthy, doughty.
ety: First attested in 1825–35. Borrowed from Chinook Jargon, from Lower Chehalis.
examples: There was a young, bold freight trainman here who tried using one of his steel-toed boots as a wheel chock. Not quite skookum enough, though. He lost a big part of his foot.
I am also configuring for the 18m tip extension, so whatever I do to the winglet attach will need to be skookum enough for the extension.

senses: Sporadic, happening infrequently and irregularly.
Consisting of a sequence of seemingly unconnected episodes.
ety: From episode + -ic. Compare French épisodique.
examples: Fortunately, my episodic bouts of dizziness didn't prevent me from climbing Chichen Itzá.
I just read five attempts at episodic novels — has nobody heard of a plot anymore?

senses: Inclined to bite.
Having a sharp or spicy flavor.
ety: From bite + -y (suffix forming adjectives). Compare West Frisian bitsich (“snappy”), Saterland Frisian bieterg (“snappish”), German Low German bittsig (“snappy”), German bissig (“snappy, snappish”).
examples: So when someone tells you their little trick for dealing with a bitey horse, just remember that that is what it is — a little trick.
It has all the beauty of an idyllic tropical island without any of the nasty, bitey stuff.

senses: Resembling the color of lead, metallic or dark gray; (of daylight) dim, overcast.
Resembling the density of lead, heavy.
Resembling the ponderousness of lead, sluggish.
ety: From Middle English leden, leaden, from Old English lēaden (“leaden, of lead”). Cognate with West Frisian leaden (“leaden”), Dutch loden (“leaden”). By surface analysis, lead + -en.
examples: The sky was dark and overcast, a leaden pall producing a deep gloom.
It was at the end of February..., when the world was cold..., when icy rains fell from the leaden skies in continual drizzling showers.
Where but to think is to be full of sorrow And leaden-eyed despairs, Where Beauty cannot keep her lustrous eyes, Or new Love pine at them beyond to-morrow.

senses: Having the status, rank or qualities of a queen; regal.
Resembling a queen (a typically feminine gay man); queenish.
ety: From Middle English queenly, quenly, from Old English cwēnlīċ, equivalent to queen + -ly.
examples: There was an innate refinement, a languid queenly hauteur about Gerty which was unmistakably evidenced in her delicate hands and higharched instep.
I'm so sorry. If I'd done my queenly duties right, none of this would have happened. But maybe I can fix it with some wish help.

senses: The track, trail, droppings, or scent of an animal.
ety: Early 19th century, from Afrikaans spoor, from Dutch spoor (“track”). Akin to Old English and Old Norse spor (whence Danish spor), and German Spur, all from Proto-Germanic *spurą. Compare spurn.
examples: We all stopped to examine that monstrous spoor. If it were indeed a bird - and what animal could leave such a mark? - its foot was so much larger than an ostrich's that its height upon the same scale must be enormous.
Even poor Nobs appeared dejected as we quit the compound and set out upon the well-marked spoor of the abductor.
Now he has picked up the spoor of drunken vomit and there is the doll sprawled against a wall, his pants streaked with urine.

senses: A boy or younger man in a homoerotic relationship with an older man.
ety: From Latin catamītus (“boy kept as a sexual partner”), from Catamītus, from Etruscan 𐌂𐌀𐌕𐌌𐌉𐌕𐌄 (catmite), from Ancient Greek Γανυμήδης (Ganumḗdēs, “Ganymede”), an attractive Trojan boy supposedly abducted to Mount Olympus by the god Zeus to become his cupbearer and lover. Doublet of Ganymede.
examples: It was the afternoon of my eighty-first birthday, and I was in bed with my catamite when Ali announced that the archbishop had come to see me.
And what about your brother? – Is he to be a catamite?

senses: A Muslim warrior who fights in war against non-Muslims, especially one who has won renown as a martial champion; often used as a title.
ety: From Arabic غَازٍ (ḡāzī, “raider, holy warrior”), from the active participle of غَزَا (ḡazā, “to raid”).
examples: Then suddenly, an hour before first light, wave after wave of screaming tribesmen, led by suicide-bent Muslim fanatics known as ghazis, began to hurl themselves against the British positions.
On a particularly joyous day of the festivities, below Our Sultan’s loge overlooking the Hippodrome, a division of impoverished frontier ghazis appeared in tattered clothes.

senses: From then on; from that time on.
ety: From thence + forward.
examples: Guestling, who adds an insatiable jealousy to his other domestic virtues, vetoed the new acquaintance and thenceforward the two met hurriedly and furtively in town.
Combpyne is 4¼ miles from Axminster, and ¼ mile beyond the station the gradient changes, the line thenceforward falling all the way to Lyme Regis.
